records.name_note: NC State's dedicated page renders an alphabetized Common Name(s) list of Saffron Spike Zebra then Zebra Plant, and lists the synonym Justicia macrophylla under 'Previously known as'; its description prose calls the species 'the zebra plant'. RHS's dedicated page gives 'zebra plant' as its profile common name (page title 'Aphelandra squarrosa | zebra plant') and lists 'saffron spike' under Other common names. Zebra Plant would be the lead, but it is already the landed common_name of a different species in this catalog, Haworthiopsis attenuata, so this record lands under the next dedicated-page lead, Saffron Spike Zebra, the first item of NC State's Common Name(s) list. RHS's 'saffron spike' is an Other common names entry and is not used as the lead.
records.toxicity_detail: No poison block on the NC State page; the only pet-safety evidence is its tag list, which carries non-toxic for cats, non-toxic for horses and non-toxic for dogs (cat and dog tags both present). No symptom list, poison parts or handling warning is given. No other admissible source reached addresses toxicity.
records.water_dry_down_target: Do not allow the soil to dry out completely
unknowns: Missouri Botanical Garden has a dedicated page (taxonid=275287) but it could not be loaded in this session (ConnectError, then a certificate error), so no MoBot claim is used. No dedicated Clemson, UF/IFAS, PSU, UMD or UGA page for Aphelandra squarrosa was found (PSU 'Zebra Plant as a Houseplant' appears to cover a different plant; UGA lists it only in a multi-species table).
Pet toxicity: only NC State's non-toxic tags name this species; they are tags, not a Poison block, and no second source corroborates.
chill_damage_f and day/night temperatures: NC State says the plant prefers temperatures that do not dip below 65 F, a preference rather than a damage-onset figure, so left null.

Sun: NC State tags Dappled Sunlight and Partial Shade (both mapped to part_shade). RHS lists Full sun and Partial shade (UK, under-glass framing); full_sun is left out because NC State's structured Light field excludes it. direct_sun_hours_max left null (the 2-6 hours is NC State's generic legend text).

Size: NC State Dimensions (Height 4-6 ft, Width 4-5 ft) is used per the anchor rule, but NC State's description ties up to 6 feet tall and 5 feet wide to its native habitat in Brazil. RHS, also a dedicated page, gives Max Height 1-1.5 metres (39.4-59.1 in) and Max Spread 1-1.5 metres, and its description says about 1.5-2m tall; indoor plants are likely to stay smaller than the NC State figures.

Fertilizing: NC State says only a weak solution every few weeks (no number or fraction), so fertilize_strength and active months are null; the 14-day interval is RHS's literal 'every 2 weeks in summer' (monthly in winter), so it applies to summer only.

Water: NC State also says 'Water frequently, not thoroughly' and 'This plant does not like wet feet', so soil_drainage stays moderate rather than moisture_retentive; RHS says 'Moist but well-drained'. Day-interval estimates and check depth are null because no source states numbers.
Soil pH: NC State's Acid (<6.0) band is open-ended, so no pH bound is set. Foot-candles, humidity percent, edibility and pollinator attraction are not addressed by the sources read.

Zebra Plant is also the landed common_name of Haworthiopsis attenuata (b6), and Goeppertia zebrina is landed as Zebra Prayer Plant (b108); this record covers Aphelandra squarrosa only and no data was borrowed from either. The research record landed this species as Zebra Plant despite the collision; the name was changed at landing (see name_note).

soil_base standard_potting rests on RHS's cultivation text, 'Grow indoors in a peat-free houseplant compost with added horticultural grit, in bright, indirect light.' Sources disagree on acidity: NC State says 'It prefers well-drained acidic potting soil.' and its Soil pH field gives Acid (<6.0), while RHS gives a standard houseplant compost and an 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' pH field.

records.toxicity_detail: Source: NC State Extension Plant Toolbox page for Polyscias fruticosa, under the Landscape > Problems heading, which lists two separate tags: "Problem for Cats" and "Problem for Dogs". The page has no Poison block, no poison-part list, no symptom list, no severity rating and no handling or skin-irritation statement, so none is reported; the tags are the page's own wording and say nothing about which part or what harm. The same page's Plant Type tags are Houseplant, Shrub, Tree; Landscape Location tags are Container, Houseplants, Patio; Resistance to Challenges is Humidity. The same page also lists Edibility: "Young leaves and shoots can be cooked as a vegetable and flavoring." and Leaf Value To Gardener tags Edible and Showy, which sits alongside the cat/dog problem tags and is not reconciled by the page; no cooking time or preparation detail is given. No other admissible source reachable in this run addressed toxicity.
records.water_dry_down_target: top 2 inches of soil dry before watering
unknowns: The Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder page for Polyscias fruticosa (taxonid=276604) could not be loaded: every fetch returned a connection error through the sandbox proxy, so MoBot supplied nothing. Clemson, UF/IFAS, PSU, UMD and UGA have no reachable dedicated page for this exact species (Clemson returned HTTP 403, the UF/IFAS FP499 guess failed, and the UGA hit was a multi-plant holiday article); none was used.

RHS page for Polyscias fruticosa is sparse: it gives other common names, synonyms, family and Name Status Correct, but no care, size, sun, soil, pH, hardiness or toxicity fields, so it supports only the name fields.

Pet toxicity rests only on NC State's Problem for Cats and Problem for Dogs tags. The page gives no poison part, symptoms, severity or skin-irritation statement, and does not say what the problem is. NC State also lists the young leaves and shoots as edible when cooked, which is not reconciled with the tags.

is_edible is true only for NC State's statement that young leaves and shoots can be cooked as a vegetable and flavoring. No cooking time or other preparation condition is given, and it should not be read as raw or whole-plant edibility given the cat/dog problem tags.

outdoor_sun_exposure is NC State's Light tag 'Partial Shade' mapped to part_shade. The page recommends it mainly as a houseplant needing bright indirect light, and outdoor use only in USDA zones 11-12. direct_sun_hours_max is left null because the 2-6 hours figure is NC State's site-wide legend text, not species prose.

Humidity: NC State says 'medium to high humidity' and tags it humidity tolerant, which straddles average and high, so humidity_need is left null. Temperatures, chill damage, light in footcandles, fertilizer, pollinators and watering-day estimates have no admissible-source support and are null.

Soil pH: NC State gives only the open-ended band 'Acid (<6.0)', so no floor or ceiling is set. soil_base is null because NC State says only 'a variety of soil types, provided it receives good drainage' (Soil Texture: Loam (Silt), Sand).

soil_drainage moderate comes from NC State's bare pair of tags Good Drainage plus Moist, together with the prose 'neither too wet nor too dry'. NC State also warns that root rot can occur in wet or overly moist soils.
NC State's Height 6-8 ft and Width 2-3 ft are converted to inches (72-96 and 24-36). Its description says up to 25 feet tall in the native habitat; the Dimensions block describes the houseplant.

name_note: RHS lists different synonyms (Aralia deleauana, Polyscias fruticosa [Ming], Polyscias 'Deleauana') from NC State's Aralia fruticosa and Panax fruticosus. This is not a hybrid. Sources agree on Ming Aralia as the lead common name, with Ming Tree second.

records.name_note: Sources split on the lead common name. MoBot's Noteworthy Characteristics prose says the plant is commonly called velvet plant or purple velvet plant. NC State's Common Name(s) list runs Purple Passion Vine, Purple Velvet Plant, Royal Velvet Plant, Velvet Plant (alphabetical), and its Description opens with Purple Velvet Plant. NC State lists 'Purple Passion' under Cultivars / Varieties as a cultivar with decumbent trailing or twining stems, the cultivar to which MoBot gives the name purple passion vine (see unknowns), so Velvet Plant, MoBot's lead name and also on NC State's list, is used here.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's page for this species has no Poison block and no symptom list. Its only pet-safety evidence is two tags in the Tags block, which reads in full: "#woody #houseplant #showy leaves #interiorscape #purple leaves #evergreen #velvety #hanging baskets #sprawling #orange flowers #hairy leaves #well-drained soil #tropical feel #non-toxic for cats #non-toxic for dogs #partial shade tolerant #container plant #malodorous". Those tags say non-toxic for cats and non-toxic for dogs. The same tag block also lists #malodorous, which refers to the flowers' unpleasant smell and is not a toxicity statement. No admissible source gives a poison-part list, a severity rating or a handling warning. MoBot says nothing about toxicity. NC State and MoBot do not address eating the plant.
unknowns: No admissible source gives pet-toxicity detail beyond NC State's two non-toxic tags: no Poison block, symptom list, poison parts or severity rating. toxic_to_pets=false rests only on those tags.
chill_damage_f left null: NC State lists USDA zones 10a-12b and MoBot says winter hardy to zones 10-12, which are survival ratings, not a damage-onset temperature.

Temperature ranges, cool-rest note, humidity, light in foot-candles, soil pH, fertilizer schedule and strength, watering day-intervals, dry-down target and check depth: no admissible source gives them for this species, so they are null.

direct_sun_hours_max left null: NC State's 2-6 hours in the Light field is the site-wide Partial Shade category legend, not species-specific prose. NC State Description says 'Bright, indirect light with protection from the afternoon sun' and MoBot says to protect it from direct afternoon sun, and neither gives hours.

outdoor_sun_exposure part_shade comes from NC State's Light field (Partial Shade). MoBot's structured Sun field also reads Part shade. Both are outdoor ratings for zones 10-12, while the plant is chiefly grown indoors in the app's context.

water_regime keep_moist rests on NC State ('Soil should be kept moist') and MoBot ('Keep soils evenly moist') watering statements. Counterpoint: MoBot's structured Water field reads Medium, which is mid-scale and does not support keep_moist on its own. Both sources also say to water less in winter and warn that overwatering may cause rot, so a rot-prone, not wet-tolerant, reading applies. soil_drainage is moderate (Good Drainage plus a moist-soil statement), not moisture_retentive, because no source asks for retentive soil.
water_dry_down_target left null: the sources frame watering as 'keep moist' with less water in winter, not as a dry-down depth.
is_edible left null: no admissible source addresses eating this species, and edibility is not inferred from the genus.
attracts_pollinators left null: neither dedicated page has an attracts or pollinator field. NC State says only that the flowers smell unpleasant and are often removed.

No RHS, Clemson or UF/IFAS page for Gynura aurantiaca was found. The RHS plant URL guesses returned 404, and the Clemson factsheet guess returned 403. RHS Name Status was therefore unavailable, and scientific_name_accepted rests on the two dedicated pages (NC State and MoBot), which both use the binomial Gynura aurantiaca.

mature_height_in and mature_spread_in come from NC State's Dimensions block (Height 1-2 ft = 12-24 in; Width 2-4 ft = 24-48 in). The page also lists Climbing Method: Twining, but it frames these as the plant's own dimensions, not a support height. MoBot's prose gives the same 2 ft by 4 ft maximum, and it frames that as size in the plant's native habitat.

MoBot's plantfinder.mobot.org host refuses non-browser clients in the automated quote checker (SKIP). MoBot quotes were checked by a browser-UA fetch of https://plantfinder.mobot.org/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=277434.

common_name researched as 'Purple Velvet Plant' (NC State's Description opener and the second name in MoBot's prose); landed as 'Velvet Plant'. Missouri Botanical Garden's page (taxonid=277434), read in a browser by the auditor and not citable from this machine, has a structured Common Name field reading 'velvet plant', and its cultivar note reads "'Purple Passion' (purple passion vine) is a decumbent cultivar featuring trailing or twining stems." unknowns: Only NC State Plant Toolbox was readable. plantfinder.mobot.org (the Missouri Botanical Garden host) failed the TLS handshake from this sandbox and could not be fetched, so no MoBot page was read. I could not locate an RHS page for Phlox stolonifera, because the RHS search is JavaScript-rendered and the guessed slug returned 404. No other admissible source with a dedicated Phlox stolonifera page was confirmed. Two cached multi-species lists (UGA Field Report, Penn State Master Gardener) mention the name but are not dedicated pages and were not used.

toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are null: the NC State page carries no Poison or Problem-for-Cats/Dogs block, and its only 'toxicity' mention is the tag 'black walnut toxicity tolerant', which concerns tolerance of juglone, not pet toxicity.

is_edible is null: NC State does not address eating this plant. is_houseplant is false: no admissible source frames it as a houseplant; NC State's Plant Type field lists Ground Cover, Native Plant and Perennial, with USDA zones 4a-8b. NC State lists a 'container plant' tag and a Container landscape location, but that is container culture, not houseplant use.

water_regime is null: NC State's description says the plant should be kept moist for the first year and is very drought tolerant once established. That is an establishment instruction plus a drought-tolerance trait, not a steady-state watering statement. Its structured Soil Drainage field (Good Drainage, Moist, Occasionally Dry) is a soil description, not a watering instruction.

soil_drainage is moderate because the NC State Soil Drainage field spans Good Drainage, Moist and Occasionally Dry, and its description reads 'moist, well-drained'. moisture_retentive was not set because no source states a humus-rich or wet-soil requirement as a cultivation requirement. The Soil Texture field does list High Organic Matter among several textures (Clay, Loam, Sand, Shallow Rocky), but that is a tolerance, not a requirement.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are null: NC State lists Acid (<6.0), Alkaline (>8.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0), so the acid and alkaline bands are open-ended and give no floor or ceiling. The prose says 'slightly acidic' but gives no number. No RHS pH field was available to check.

outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State's structured Light field lists Full sun, Partial Shade and Deep shade, which map to full_sun, part_shade and full_shade. The description says the plant performs best in full sun to partial shade. Only one admissible source was read, so there was no second source to cross-check against.
direct_sun_hours_max is null: the only hour figures on the page are the generic hour ranges inside the Light category labels, and the species prose gives no maximum hours.
soil_base garden_bed reflects an in-ground groundcover/perennial use per NC State's description and landscape fields, not a stated potting-mix recommendation.

Humidity, temperature, chill damage, fertilizer and light in foot-candles are null because there is no admissible-source support. NC State gives USDA zones 4a-8b, which is a hardiness range and not a damage-onset temperature.

Phlox subulata, landed in this catalog as Moss Phlox (b41), is also commonly called creeping phlox, and Phlox divaricata is landed as Woodland Phlox (b51); NC State names both in this page's 'is often confused with' module. All content here is from the Phlox stolonifera page only.

records.name_note: Sources differ on the lead common name. MoBot's Noteworthy Characteristics prose and RHS's page title give Stokes' aster. NC State's Common Name(s) list reads Cornflower Aster, Stoke's Aster, Stokes' Aster, an alphabetized list in the same order as its page-title parenthetical, so Cornflower Aster comes first there; NC State's description prose uses the spelling Stoke’s aster. Stokes' Aster was chosen because it leads at MoBot and RHS and is one of NC State's three names.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets, toxicity_detail and is_edible are null: the NC State page for this species carries no Poison block and no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags, and none of the admissible pages read addresses toxicity to cats or dogs or eating the plant. UF/IFAS, Penn State, UMD and UGA were not found to have a Stokesia page and no toxicity record was found on them.

Wet-winter statements as worded: MoBot Culture says 'Wet soil in winter is the main cause of death for this plant. A well-drained soil is essential.' RHS Cultivation says 'liable to rot in wet winter soils'. NC State separately says it 'will tolerate occasionally wet soil'. soil_drainage is therefore moderate (NC State Good Drainage + Moist + Occasionally Wet; MoBot and RHS well-drained), not fast and not moisture_retentive.

outdoor_sun_exposure lists only full_sun. NC State lists Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours) as a structured Light value, and its prose says 'Stoke’s aster grows in full sun to partial shade'. MoBot's structured Sun field and RHS's Position field are Full sun only, and MoBot's prose says 'Tolerates filtered sunlight, but prefers full sun'. Clemson says it will tolerate some part shade. part_shade is left out because the two other sources' structured sun fields exclude it, and that is disclosed here.
direct_sun_hours_max is null: no species-specific prose gives a maximum; NC State's 6-or-more hours is its site-wide light-category legend.

water_regime is null: MoBot's structured 'Water: Medium' is mid-scale and does not support keep_moist; NC State 'prefers moist soil with good drainage' and MoBot 'average, medium moisture' are soil adjectives, not watering statements. water_* day fields, water_dry_down_target and fertilizer fields are null for an in-ground perennial with no source framing.

soil_ph_min is null because NC State's Acid (<6.0) band is open-ended. soil_ph_max 8.0 is the closed top of NC State's Neutral (6.0-8.0) band; RHS lists pH as Acid or Neutral (no alkaline), so the ceiling is not contradicted.

Size conflict: NC State Dimensions give 1-2 ft tall and 1-1.5 ft wide (used, in inches 12-24 and 12-18). RHS gives Max Height 0.1-0.5 metres and Max Spread 0.1-0.5 metres (3.9-19.7 in), a different, smaller range; MoBot gives 1.00 to 2.00 feet tall and 1.00 to 1.50 feet spread, matching NC State.
RHS's Cultivation sentence is on the Stokesia laevis page; the genus is monotypic. The sentence also appears on cultivar pages.

chill_damage_f is null: the zone 5-9 and RHS H4 ratings are survival ratings, not damage-onset temperatures. Temperature, humidity and indoor light fields are null (garden perennial; no admissible source states them).
